newsitem.title: USA: Arizona governor admits errors in days as developer.
newsitem.headline: Arizona governor admits errors in days as developer.

text.p: Gov. Fife Symington, fighting for his political life, acknowledged Tuesday that he made frequent mistakes on the information he gave to lenders in his days as a prominent developer.
In a packed federal courtroom, Symington repeatedly said he used incorrect values on statements given to various financial institutions because he was not paying attention to details.
But he stressed that the errors involving office projects, hotels and even his own home were not meant to deceptive.
"The financial statement was not the focus of my life," he told the jurors.

The two-term Republican governor attempted to explain other apparent discrepancies pointed out by prosecutors, saying the values assigned to certain real estate holdings were based on what he thought they would reap in the future, not now.
"In hindsight, it can be criticised," Symington told jurors when asked about his aggressive estimates.

The differing numbers are at the heart of the case against Symington, who is charged with 22 counts of fraud, attempted extortion and perjury. He would be ousted from office if convicted on even a single count, and could face a possible prison sentence.
With methodical cross-examination, prosecutors spent Tuesday trying to prove that Symington deliberately lied to lenders to save his crumbling real estate empire in the mid-1980s to early 1990s.
The testimony was punctuated with several testy exchanges between Symington and U.S. Assistant Attorney David Schindler.

Prosecutors took Symington document by document through his finances attempting to show that the then-developer gave different stories to different lenders, puffing up his bottom line to secure loans and deflating it when he sought forgiveness.
The government claims Symington attempted to extort loan concessions from labour union pension funds. The union loaned $10 million for a shopping centre in downtown Phoenix.
Symington, who filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy in September 1995, also is charged with lying during the court proceedings.
He was expected to resume his testimony Wednesday.
